text:
# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–15 (Complete – Updated 117)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Autumn of fourth year (Chapter 15 heading). Earlier: Early morning of Waterloo campaign battle day—Regiment receives marching orders; troops march within hours. French crossed Sambre; British left engaged. Bugle signals at dawn; Brussels awakens to drums and pipes. Regiment departs in early morning; sun rising. After departure: Jos remains in Brussels commanding small establishment; Amelia invalided; sun high in heavens; regiment miles on march before Jos appears at breakfast.**
- **Earlier Timeline**: Spring of fourth year with Seena Orlwood drowned; Winter of third year with frost; Evening at Brighton; Fine moonlight night of May; Army ordered to Belgium; Transports to Ostend; Amelia and Jos to Ramsgate; Belgium in happy season transitioning to war; Famous Brussels ball evening of 15 June 1815 (historical).
- **Primary Locations**: London (Russell Square, Thames Street, Slaughters' hotel, Gray's Inn Square, Hulker and Bullock bankers), Brighton, Mirecombe, Wilhaven, Chatham, Harwich, Fulham, Ramsgate, Ostend, Brussels (Hotel de Ville, Park, Hotel du Parc, opera-house, restaurateur's, Place of Arms), Belgium, Salwick harbor town, Salford, Miremere.

## Main Characters

**Captain William Dobbin** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Critical Actions - Departure Morning**: Came to Jos's quarters at dawn before regiment's departure while George occupied with own affairs and grief at parting. Roused Jos from sleep; insisted on shaking hands before departure. Instructed Jos with utmost seriousness: "We march in a quarter of an hour, Sedley, and neither George nor I may ever come back. You are not to stir from this town until you ascertain how things go. Stay here and watch over your sister, and comfort her, and see that no harm comes to her. If anything happens to George, remember she has no one but you in the world to look to. If it goes wrong with the army, you'll see her safe back to England; you will promise me on your word that you will never desert her. I know you won't." Asked if Jos needed gold to return to England in case of misfortune. **Expected personal comfort from one more view of Amelia before departure; his selfishness was punished. Saw her wrapped in white morning dress, hair falling on shoulders, large eyes fixed and without light, holding George's sash against bosom from which heavy net of crimson dropped like stain of blood. "Good God," thought he, "and is it grief like this I dared to pry into?" Stood powerless and torn with pity. Dobbin's mind was perfectly set at ease that Jos had spoken resolutely respecting conduct to his sister: "At least," thought the Captain, "there will be a retreat secured for her in case the worst should ensue."**
- **Earlier Actions**: At play-table during ball aftermath, whispered to George about Sambre crossing and left engagement; George responded with wild hurray. Arrived Brighton via Slaughters' hotel; dined with officers; assumed jovial manner hiding feelings. In George's room: delivered disinheritance letter; George erupted; Dobbin offered financial support. At Chatham: wore shells on frockcoat, crimson sash and sabre; recognized Amelia; never spoke during Mrs. O'Dowd's party; took Jos home (maudlin); handed Amelia into carriage (she rebuked him smilingly); loitered smoking cigar watching George's windows; bought piano for Amelia's father's house at Fulham. In Belgium: "In a rage" at treatment of Amelia by Lady Blanche Thistlewood and Countess of Bareacres; accompanied Jos and Amelia on carriage drives; at opera shrieked with laughter when Rebecca kissed fingers, again when Mrs. O'Dowd mistakenly took compliment; Rebecca leaned on his arm returning to her box. Few days after opera: remonstrated with George about giving up play. At famous Brussels ball: only person who disturbed Amelia's unhappy thoughts; brought refreshments, sat beside her; when Amelia clung to him (called him by Christian name), she begged him to take her home; he went away with her quickly through crowds.
- **Internal Conflict**: Deeply troubled by guilt over hastening marriage. Secret adoration of Amelia is his "greatest privilege and hope of life"; privately resolved he would not have let her go to Belgium if married to her. Knows Amelia considers him plain, awkward, ungainly. Now avoided by George in public.
- **Reputation**: "Greatly respected in the regiment, as the best officer and the cleverest man in it"

**George Osborne** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Final Departure**: **At sound of stirring call to battle, jumped away from gentle arms in which he had been dallying; felt shame that he should have been detained so long. Same feeling of eagerness and excitement was amongst all his friends. The sun was just rising as march began—gallant sight—band led column playing regimental march; Major in command riding upon Pyramus; grenadiers marched with Captain at head; colours borne by senior and junior Ensigns in centre; George came marching at head of his company. He looked up, smiled at Amelia, and passed on; even sound of music died away.**
- **Critical Final Hours**: Upon receiving Dobbin's news at play-table, gave wild hurray, clapped glass on table, walked away speedily. Nerves quivered with excitement at long-looked-for news; thought about thousand things—past life, future chances, fate before him, wife, child perhaps from whom unseen he might part. Wished night's work undone and could say farewell to tender and guileless being by whose love he had set such little store. Thought over brief married life; in few weeks had frightfully dissipated little capital; had been wild and reckless. If mischance befall him, what left for her? How unworthy he was. Remembered father's generosity. Sat down and wrote farewell letter to father (remembering duel engagement letter reference). Dawn streaked sky as he closed letter; sealed and kissed superscription; thought how he deserted generous father and thousand kindnesses. **Had looked into Amelia's bedroom when entered from ball; she lay quiet with eyes seemed closed; he was glad she was asleep. Upon arriving at quarters, found regimental servant already making departure preparations. Debated whether to wake Amelia or leave note for Jos. Went in to look at her once again. She had been awake when he first entered but kept eyes closed so wakefulness should not seem to reproach him. When he returned after herself, her timid heart felt more at ease; she turned towards him, fell into light sleep. George came in and looked again, entering more softly. By pale night-lamp could see her sweet pale face—purple eyelids fringed and closed; one round arm smooth and white lay outside coverlet. He saw how pure, gentle, tender, friendless she was; how selfish, brutal, black with crime he was. Heart-stained and shame-stricken, stood at bed's foot. Came to bedside, looked at little soft hand; bent over pillow noiselessly toward gentle pale face. Two fair arms closed tenderly round his neck as he stooped down.**
- **Earlier Status**: Married Amelia late April without father's consent; disinherited (determination "final and irrevocable"). Receives £2,000 in 4 percent annuities and £100/year widow's allowance for Amelia. Lost £140 to Rawdon at cards; obtained £2,000 cheque from Hulker and Bullock bankers. At Chatham: sent Amelia to mother with carte blanche; paid for everything requisite. At Brussels: ashamed of regiment, resolved to exchange to better regiment soon; takes wife to nightly jaunts; quite pleased with himself. Danced with Lady Blanche Thistlewood and Rebecca at ball. Called upon ladies; rode in Park; asked their party to dinner at restaurateur's. Purchased horse for private riding. Told Amelia Rebecca is comfort to "get rid of this damn'd Irishwoman" (Mrs. O'Dowd). Carrying on "desperate flirtation" with Rebecca; rides with her whenever free; pretends regimental business to Amelia (by which falsehood she not deceived); consigns wife to solitude or Jos's society; passes evenings in Crawleys' company; loses money to Rawdon; flatters himself wife "dying of love for him." At opera: claimed "We bear the same arms" to General Tufto; Rebecca left his box giving "queerest, knowingest look." After opera: Dobbin criticized Rebecca; George defended her. Few days after opera: told Dobbin "we play low; I won last night" and suggested Crawley does not cheat; plays repeatedly with Crawley now. General Tufto dines abroad almost constantly; George always welcome in Crawley's apartments.

**Amelia Osborne** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Departure and After**: **During George's final departure preparations, wrapped in white morning dress, hair falling on shoulders, large eyes fixed and without light. By way of helping and showing she could be useful at critical moment, took up sash of George's from drawers and followed him to and fro with sash in hand, looking on mutely as his packing proceeded. Came out and stood leaning at wall, holding sash against bosom, from which heavy net of crimson dropped like large stain of blood. Dobbin felt guilty shock at sight. At sound of stirring call to battle, George jumped away from her gentle arms. After departure: invalided; remained for hours silent, motionless, and haggard by windows in which she placed herself to watch last bayonets of column as it marched away. Amelia's attendant (Pauline the cook), finding her condition, consoled her more than anybody; when found Amelia remained hours at window, honest girl took lady's hand and said Pauline's own man was also in the army; burst into tears; Amelia falling into her arms did likewise; each pitied and soothed other.**
- **Earlier Status**: Troubled by Rebecca's wit and misgivings about her. Rose early at Chatham; packed trunks with "greatest alacrity" while George lay in bed. Mother clasped her to heart with "all maternal eagerness and affection." Knelt seeking spiritual consolation. Bustling about completing outfit with great taste and elegant discernment. Adopted by regiment with acclamation. In Belgium: natural and unaffected; only amused by Mrs. O'Dowd's eccentricities. Letters home filled with delight and gratitude. Husband bade her buy laces, millinery, jewels; he kindest, best, most generous of men. At general's party: Countess of Bareacres would not answer; Lady Blanche stared with eye-glass; Amelia wrote piteous accounts home. At opera: gentle eyes fixed anxiously on Rebecca and George; embraced Rebecca with affectionate rapture. When visited Rawdon and Rebecca's quarters: displayed evident unwillingness and high and mighty manner; George scolded her violently; she silent but more bashful and awkward on second visit. Not quite six weeks married. Aware George carrying on flirtation with Rebecca; does not plague him with jealousy but becomes unhappy and pines miserably in secret. At Brussels ball: did not know soul; sat quite unnoticed in corner except when Rawdon came and Dobbin brought refreshments. Alarmed by Rebecca telling her George would go on playing. Witnessing Rebecca's request to George for scarf and flowers (done twenty times before in last few days) proved "quite too much for her"; suddenly clung to Dobbin called him by Christian name, begged him to take her home; went away with him quickly through crowds; did not sleep that night.

**Captain Rawdon Crawley** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Departure and Character Demonstrated**: At sound of stirring call to battle, same feeling of eagerness and excitement was amongst all those friends. Upon receiving final news that campaign was opened and troops to march, gravity became such that Rebecca rallied him, which hurt his feelings. Said with tremor in voice: "You don't suppose I'm afraid, Becky, I should think. But I'm a pretty good mark for a shot, and you see if it brings me down, why I leave one and perhaps two behind me whom I should wish to provide for, as I brought 'em into the scrape. It is no laughing matter that, Mrs. C., anyways." This showed genuine concern—previously had seldom thought about anything but himself until last few months when Love obtained mastery over dragoon. Made last dispositions: went through various items of little catalogue of effects, striving to see how they might be turned into money for Rebecca's benefit in case any accident should befall him. Dressed himself in oldest and shabbiest uniform and epaulets, leaving newest behind under wife's (or it might be his widow's) guardianship. This famous dandy of Windsor and Hyde Park went off on campaign with kit as modest as that of sergeant, and with something like prayer on his lips for woman he was leaving. Took her up from ground, held her in his arms for minute, tight pressed against strong-beating heart. Face was purple and eyes dim as he put her down and left her. Rode by his General's side, smoked cigar in silence as they hastened after troops of General's brigade, which preceded them; not until some miles on their way that he left off twirling moustache and broke silence.
- **Earlier Status**: Secretly married to Rebecca; heavily indebted. Extracted considerable payment from George in bank-notes and bill on agents; lost £140 to George at cards. Met Miss Crawley when she took air in chair; she held out couple of fingers; Rawdon turned red as scarlet. Miss Crawley subsequently disparaged his appearance. In Belgium: Now in Brussels lodging at Hotel du Parc with Rebecca and General Tufto. Encountered Osborne party in park; shook hands heartily with Amelia and spoke warmly to Jos; stared at Mrs. O'Dowd's face and black cock's feathers until she thought she made conquest. Sent message to George at opera inviting him to dinner Tuesday when General dines out; asked George to "make Sedley cut off his moustache." Said "Hm, as you please" when George expressed intention to pay respects to Rebecca alone, looking very glum; two young officers exchanged knowing glances. Repeatedly together with George now; George always welcome in quarters. Lets Osborne come and go with entire good humour; understood perfectly well with Rebecca (though never absolutely conspired in so many words) that one cajoled young gentleman whilst other won his money at cards.

**Rebecca Sharp (Mrs. Rebecca Rawdon Crawley)** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Post-Departure Actions**: Wisely determined not to give way to unavailing sentimentality on Rawdon's departure. Waved him adieu from window, stood there moment looking out after he was gone. Cathedral towers and full gables of quaint old houses were just beginning to blush in sunrise. Had been no rest for her that night. Still in her pretty ball-dress, fair hair hanging somewhat out of curl on her neck, circles round her eyes dark with watching. Put bouquet of ball into glass of water and went to bed and slept very comfortably. Found in Rawdon's pocket-book draft for twenty pounds on Osborne's banker. Determined to get it cashed and pay visit afterwards to "poor little Emmy." Passed morning disposing, ordering, looking out, and locking up her properties in most agreeable manner. Made calculations of Rawdon's valuables; found with pungent feeling of triumph and self-satisfaction that should circumstances occur, she might reckon on six or seven hundred pounds at very least, to begin world with. **After departing from Jos: went to visit Amelia. Upon arrival without ringing at antechamber door, found Jos in braided frock attempting to dress; Rebecca laughed at his attitude and convulsions in donning coat. Dressed very neatly and smartly as usual; her quiet sleep had refreshed her; pink smiling cheeks quite pleasant to look at in town and on day when everybody else's countenance wore deepest anxiety and gloom. Asked: "Are you preparing to join the army, Mr. Joseph?" and "Is there to be nobody left in Brussels to protect us poor women?" Inquired how Amelia was "after the events of the morning--after the fatigues of the ball the night before?"**
- **Rebecca Manipulates Jos**: **Made speech that might be interpreted, "My dear sir, should an accident befall the army, and a retreat be necessary, you have a very comfortable carriage, in which I propose to take a seat." Told Jos: "You men can bear anything. Parting or danger are nothing to you. Own now that you were going to join the army and leave us to our fate. I know you were--something tells me you were. I was so frightened, when the thought came into my head (for I do sometimes think of you when I am alone, Mr. Joseph), that I ran off immediately to beg and entreat you not to fly from us." Professed: "You men would sacrifice anything for a pleasure. Captain Crawley left me this morning as gay as if he were going to a hunting party. What does he care? What do any of you care for the agonies and tortures of a poor forsaken woman? Oh! dear Mr. Sedley, I have come to you for comfort--for consolation. I have been on my knees all the morning. I tremble at the frightful danger into which our husbands, our friends, our brave troops and allies, are rushing. And I come here for shelter, and find another of my friends--the last remaining to me--bent upon plunging into the dreadful scene!" Told Jos: "I know you think me ungrateful. Your coldness, your averted looks, your manner when we have met of late--when I came in just now, all proved it to me. But were there no reasons why I should avoid you? Let your own heart answer that question. Do you think my husband was too much inclined to welcome you? The only unkind words I have ever had from him (I will do Captain Crawley that justice) have been about you--and most cruel, cruel words they were." Jos's blood tingled with delight; his heart inflamed again; doubts and suspicions forgotten. Rebecca thought: "If the worst comes to the worst, my retreat is secure; and I have a right-hand seat in the barouche." When Isidor reappeared and Jos was about to gasp out avowal, Rebecca kissed her hand to Jos and said "Au revoir," then tapped gently at Amelia's apartment door to comfort her; Jos sank down in chair, gazed and sighed and puffed portentously.**
- **Earlier Status**: Secretly married to Rawdon; heavily indebted. Successfully reconciled with Miss Briggs on beach. Sent crumpled note to Rawdon requesting money from "Cupid" (George); Rawdon extracted considerable payment; remarked "comfortable inn in Brighton is better than spunging-house in Chancery Lane." Packed chief valuables sent to London under care of George's servant. In Belgium: Now in Brussels with Rawdon and General Tufto at Hotel du Parc. Encountered Osborne party in Park riding on beautiful little Arab in prettiest tightest riding-habit (acquired art at Queen's Crawley); accompanied by General Tufto amid greatest persons in Brussels. Acknowledged Amelia graciously with nod, smile, playful finger-kissing. At opera: performed hand-kissing toward Amelia's box; clapped hands when George entered her box; General Tufto's presence noted—he stared at George with sulky scowl. Rebecca left box leaning on Dobbin's arm. During her time in Amelia's box, bustled, chattered, turned and twisted, smiled upon one, smirked on another; admired Mrs. O'Dowd's Cairngorm brooch and Irish diamonds. After opera, General Tufto cursed "so deep, that no compositor would venture to print them"; was jealous and angry. Osborne and Crawley repeatedly together now; George always welcome in their apartments. When Amelia and George visited, Amelia displayed evident unwillingness; nearly caused first quarrel; George scolded Amelia violently; Amelia bashful and awkward on second visit. Rebecca remarked to George: thought Amelia jealous at Brighton; now supposes scandalized because Rawdon, Rebecca, and General live together; questioned how they could live without friend to share expenses; claimed she was "very much obliged to Emmy, very"; revealed General ready to "eat me for going with you to visit that foolish little wife of yours"; pert toss of head; invited George to dinner; General dines with Commander-in-Chief. At Brussels ball: invited; danced with George twice or thrice; made request to George for scarf and flowers (done twenty times before in last few days). Later at hotel after ball: Rebecca and Rawdon discussed financial schemes—Rebecca saying "we have not done with your aunt yet; if she fails us, isn't there what you call the Gazette? or when your uncle Bute's life drops, I have another scheme. Living has always belonged to younger brother, why shouldn't you sell out and go into the Church?" Idea of conversion set Rawdon into roars of laughter (explosion heard through hotel at midnight); General Tufto heard haw-haws of great dragoon's voice from quarters on first floor above them; Rebecca acted scene with great spirit and preached Rawdon's first sermon to immense delight of General at breakfast.

**Jos Sedley** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Current Status - After Departure and Rebecca's Visit**: **Left in command of little colony at Brussels with Amelia invalided, Isidor (Belgian servant), and bonne (maid-of-all-work) as garrison under him. Rest broken by sounding of bugles in early morning. Though disturbed in spirit and rest destroyed by Dobbin's interruption and morning's occurrences, nevertheless remained for many hours in bed, wakeful and rolling about until usual hour of rising arrived. Sun high in heavens and regiment miles on their march before civilian appeared in flowered dressing-gown at breakfast. Amelia could not come to breakfast and cut tartines Jos liked; Madame was great deal too ill and had been in frightful state ever since husband's departure, so her bonne said. Jos showed his sympathy by pouring her out large cup of tea; improved on this; not only sent her breakfast, but bethought him what delicacies she would most like for dinner. After Isidor warned him about wearing military coat (Frenchmen have sworn not to give quarter to single British soldier), Jos told Isidor: "Give me my coat and cap, sir, and follow me. I will go myself and learn the truth of these reports." Jos was, if not seriously alarmed as yet, at least considerably disturbed in mind. Put on braided frock with resolute countenance and indomitable resolution, thrust his arm into the sleeve. During this heroic act, Mrs. Rawdon Crawley arrived to visit Amelia. Succeeded in plunging into the coat and came forward blushing and stuttering out excuses to his fair visitor. Rebecca laughed at his attitude. She asked if he was preparing to join the army and if there would be nobody left in Brussels to protect poor women. Jos was profoundly mortified by Rebecca's inattention to him during their stay at Brussels—never presented to any of Rawdon Crawley's great acquaintances; scarcely invited to her parties; too timid to play much; his presence bored George and Rawdon equally. But now Rebecca's words and knowing tender glances inflamed his heart again; all doubts and suspicions forgotten. A few adroit words from Rebecca caused Jos's blood to tingle with delight at surveying this victim to his attractions. Was about to gasp out avowal when Isidor reappeared and began to busy himself about domestic affairs. Jos choked almost with emotion obliged to restrain. When Rebecca left to comfort Amelia, saying "Au revoir" and kissing her hand, Jos sank down in a chair, gazed and sighed and puffed portentously. His thoughts now glowed, maddening, upon contemplation of enchanting Rebecca; anon shrinking guiltily before vision of jealous Rawdon Crawley with his curling, fierce mustachios and terrible duelling pistols loaded and cocked. Isidor remarked: "That coat is very tight for Milor," but Jos heard him not; his thoughts were elsewhere.**
- **Earlier Status**: Arrived Chatham in fine carriage with Amelia; recognized Dobbin; attended Mrs. O'Dowd's party in maudlin state; told tiger-hunt story. Agreed to escort Amelia and Mrs. O'Dowd abroad; ceased shaving upper lip; followed parades and drills with great assiduity; received excellent assistance from Mrs. O'Dowd in military studies. Made appearance in braided frock-coat and duck trousers, foraging cap with smart gold band. In Belgium: Interposed about curry and rice; owned with sigh that England had no equal for good streaky beef despite Mrs. O'Dowd's assertions. Hired pair of horses for open carriage in Brussels; made tolerable figure in drives about Park. Accompanied Amelia on carriage drives; more at ease when great man (General Tufto with Rebecca) departed. Referenced Battle of Salamanca. At opera: eating ice; Rebecca admired Jos with "kindliest greeting." At Brussels ball: panting to be asked with Mrs. O'Dowd; strove in vain to procure tickets; made Jos envious when Dobbin displayed invitation.

**Mrs. Major Peggy O'Dowd** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- One of five sisters and eleven children of Glenmalony. Upon understanding regiment will march next morning, became very grave. Major told her to wake him half an hour before assembly beats, call him at half-past one, prepare his things; may be he'll not come back to breakfast (signifying regiment will march next morning). After regiment's departure, betook herself to large volume of uncle the Dean's sermons for meditation; perhaps did not understand much; thoughts were elsewhere; sleep project with poor Mick's nightcap on pillow was quite vain one. She who remains and suffers—has leisure to think, brood, remember.
- In Brussels: continually prattles about Ballinasloe, Dublin cattle, markets, Glenmalony. Cock's plume in hat and large repeater on stomach. Not invited to Brussels ball; panted to be asked; strove in vain to procure tickets; made Jos envious when Dobbin displayed invitation. At opera: wore splendid Irish diamonds and Cairngorms; tossed about fan with splendid complacency; when Rebecca performed hand-kissing, Mrs. O'Dowd mistakenly took compliment to herself and returned gracious smile, sending Dobbin shrieking from box. Rebecca admired her brooch and diamonds, wouldn't believe they were not from Golconda direct. Made timely observation when neither lady rallied ("Why didn't you BOY one?" regarding bouquets); became silent and subdued afterward.

**Major Mick O'Dowd** [MINOR CHARACTER]
- Served sovereign in every quarter of world; paid for every step by acts of daring and gallantry. Most modest, silent, sheep-faced, meek of little men; obedient to wife. Upon understanding regiment will march next morning, placidly pulled nightcap over his ears, told Peggy: "that there will be such a ball danced in a day or two as some of 'em has never heard the chune of"; much more happy to retire to rest after quiet tumbler than figure at other sort of amusement. Asked to be woken half an hour before assembly beats, called at half-past one, things ready; may be he'll not come back to breakfast; words signified opinion that regiment would march next morning; ceased talking and fell asleep.

**Isidor (Belgian Servant)** [MINOR CHARACTER]
- **Current Post-Departure Attitude**: Looked on very sulkily while Osborne's servant was disposing of his master's baggage previous to Captain's departure. In first place hated Mr. Osborne, whose conduct to him and to all inferiors was generally overbearing (nor does continental domestic like to be treated with insolence as own better-tempered servants do); secondly, was angry that so many valuables should be removed from under his hands, to fall into other people's possession when English discomfiture should arrive. Of this defeat he and vast number of other persons in Brussels and Belgium did not make slightest doubt. Almost universal belief was that Emperor would divide Prussian and English armies, annihilate one after other, and march into Brussels before three days were over: when all movables of present masters, who would be killed, or fugitives, or prisoners, would lawfully become property of Monsieur Isidor. Jos knows nothing of what passing in domestic's mind; Isidor marking his victim down, as one of Mr. Paynter's assistants in Leadenhall Street ornaments unconscious turtle with placard on which is written, "Soup to-morrow." **After Dobbin's departure, served Jos by removing flowered dressing-gown. When Jos became disturbed and put on braided frock to learn truth of reports about French advance and Duchess fleeing Brussels, Isidor became furious and remonstrated: "Milor had better not wear that military coat. The Frenchmen have sworn not to give quarter to a single British soldier." When Jos insisted on dressing despite warning, Isidor disappeared into adjacent bedroom bearing off flowered dressing-gown. Later, when Jos and Rebecca were together, Isidor made his reappearance and began to busy himself about domestic affairs, interrupting moment when Jos was about to gasp out avowal to Rebecca. Isidor remarked: "That coat is very tight for Milor," still having his eye on the frogs.**
- **Servant's Intelligence and Reports to Jos**: Informed Jos: "His papers are burned, his effects are removed, and his quarters are being got ready for the Duke of Dalmatia. I had it from his own maitre d'hotel. Milor Duc de Richemont's people are packing up everything. His Grace has fled already, and the Duchess is only waiting to see the plate packed to join the King of France at Ostend." Became self-declared partisan of Napoleon; took proclamation from his pocket and sternly thrust it into his master's face; already looked upon frogged coat and valuables as his own spoil. Said: "The Prussians were three to one at Jena, and he took their army and kingdom in a week. They were six to one at Montmirail, and he scattered them like sheep. The Austrian army is coming, but with the Empress and the King of Rome at its head; and the Russians, bah! the Russians will withdraw. No quarter is to be given to the English, on account of their cruelty to our braves on board the infamous pontoons. Look here, here it is in black and white. Here's the proclamation of his Majesty the Emperor and King."

**Pauline (Cook)** [MINOR CHARACTER]
- Amelia's attendant. Much less selfishly disposed than Isidor. Few dependents could come near Amelia, kind and gentle creature, without paying usual tribute of loyalty and affection to her sweet and affectionate nature. When found Amelia remained for hours silent, motionless, and haggard by windows watching last bayonets of column march away, honest girl took lady's hand and said Pauline's own man was also in the army; burst into tears; Amelia falling into her arms did likewise; each pitied and soothed other.

**John Osborne (Old Mr. Osborne)** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- Wealthy merchant; George's father; savage, determined man. Upon learning George married Amelia, erupted in fury. Locked himself in study; retrieved mahogany escritoire; examined George's documents with "curses quivering on livid lips" and "horrid hatred and disappointment"; marked, docketed, catalogued with dates. Commissioned lawyer to draft letter stating determination "final and irrevocable." George ceases to be family member. News how son is entertaining peers and peeresses came to Osborne's ears in the City. George wrote farewell letter to him at dawn before regiment's departure, remembering his past generosity and thousand kindnesses, sealed and kissed superscription.

**General Tufto** [MINOR CHARACTER]
- Military officer in Brussels with considerable status. Lodging at Hotel du Parc with Rawdon and Rebecca. Dines out almost constantly; Tuesday mentioned as occasion dining with Commander-in-Chief. At opera: stared at George with sulky scowl when George entered Rebecca's box; disengaged eye working round in Rebecca's direction, shooting out bloodshot glances at her and George; when Rebecca left box with George, gave low utterance to curses "so deep, that no compositor would venture to print them"; curses came from heart; was jealous and angry; ready to "eat me for going with you to visit that foolish little wife of yours" (Amelia). Capable of generating such lust and fury, rage and hatred. Heard roars of laughter from Rawdon and Rawdon's haw-haws through hotel at midnight (Rebecca's Church conversion scene preached to him at breakfast, to immense delight).

**Nynelle Hollmere, Lutho Hollmere, Fetho** [MINOR CHARACTERS]
- **Chapter 15 fragments**: Lutho Hollmere walked the long way round to avoid the muddy square; laughed at a story nobody else found funny. Fetho mended a torn sleeve by the window and said little; talked of nothing much with Ulvie—the weather, the harvest, a lame horse. Nynelle Hollmere found work in Miremere, moved there, and did not return to Salwick. **[NARRATOR'S NOTE: These fragments appear to be narrative intrusions or background texture; unclear connection to main plot.]**

## Critical Facts and Status

**WATERLOO CAMPAIGN - BATTLE COMMENCED AND REGIMENT DEPARTED**: French have crossed Sambre; British left already engaged. Regiment receives marching orders in early morning hours. Sun just rising as march began—gallant sight—band led column playing regimental march; Major in command riding upon Pyramus; grenadiers marched with Captain at head; colours borne by senior and junior Ensigns in centre; George came marching at head of his company. He looked up, smiled at Amelia, and passed on; even sound of music died away. **Regiment now miles on their march; Jos left in command of Brussels establishment with Amelia invalided, Isidor, and bonne as garrison under him.**

**GEORGE-AMELIA MARRIAGE - SEVERED AT CRITICAL MOMENT**: Married late April; disinherited "final and irrevocable"; receives £2,000 in 4 percent annuities and £100/year widow's allowance for Amelia. Not quite six weeks married. George carrying on "desperate flirtation" with Rebecca. At final moment before departure: George bent over Amelia's bedside after she roused; she awoke and threw her fair arms round his neck with sob, saying "I am awake, George"; at that moment bugle from Place of Arms began sounding clearly, taken up through town; amidst drums and pipes, whole city awoke; George departed with regiment. **After departure: Amelia invalided; remained for hours silent, motionless, and haggard by windows watching last bayonets of column march away; Pauline the cook consoled her; both wept together; each pitied and soothed other.**

**REBECCA'S CUNNING AND MANIPULATION - EXPANDS**: Upon Rawdon's departure, wisely determined not to give way to sentimentality. Waved him adieu from window and went to bed and slept comfortably. Found draft for twenty pounds on Osborne's banker in Rawdon's pocket-book; determined to get it cashed and visit "poor little Emmy." Made calculations of Rawdon's valuables; found she might reckon on six or seven hundred pounds at very least to begin world with. Passed morning disposing, ordering, looking out, and locking up her properties. Narrator marks her as "indomitable little aide-de-camp's wife"—as cool and collected as great Duke himself in presence of doubts and difficulties. **After visiting Jos (whom she flattered and manipulated into emotional state with false sympathy and strategically placed remarks), Rebecca went to comfort Amelia, securing Jos's continued emotional investment and establishing secure retreat with him should army be defeated. Rebecca's calculation: "If the worst comes to the worst, my retreat is secure; and I have a right-hand seat in the barouche."**

**BELGIAN AND BRUSSELS STAFF ASSESSMENTS - DEEPENS**: Isidor and vast number of other persons in Brussels and Belgium did not make slightest doubt of English discomfiture. Almost universal belief was that Emperor would divide Prussian and English armies, annihilate one after other, and march into Brussels before three days were over. Jos knows nothing of what passing in servants' minds; they marking him down for plunder when English are defeated. **Isidor now openly declares himself partisan of Napoleon; believes Belgian nobility fleeing (Duchess, Duc de Richemont) confirm inevitable French victory.**
